title: Split Strings by Separator
statement:
You get a list of strings `words` and one character `separator`. Cut every string of `words` at each place where `separator` appears; the separator itself belongs to none of the pieces, and one string can break into many pieces.

Return a single list holding all the pieces, ordered first by the position of the string they came from in `words` and then by their position inside that string. Pieces that are empty (from a leading, trailing or repeated separator) are left out, so the answer may be an empty list.
constraints: Each words[i] contains only lowercase English letters and the characters . , | $ # @
separator is one of the characters . , | $ # @
notes:
## Intuition

Each word can be read left to right while a growing `piece` collects ordinary characters. A separator marks the end of a piece, and the end of the word does too. Whenever a piece ends, it goes into the answer only if it holds at least one character; that one check removes every empty piece produced by separators at the start, at the end, or side by side. A built-in `split` followed by a filter does the same job and is a fine brute force.

## Approach

1. Start an empty `result` list.
2. For each `word`, reset `piece` to the empty string.
3. Walk the characters `ch` of the word. If `ch` is the separator, push `piece` when it is non-empty and reset it; otherwise append `ch` to `piece`.
4. After the last character, push the leftover `piece` if it is non-empty.
5. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`separator = "."`. In `"one.two.three"` the piece grows to `"one"`, the first dot pushes it, `"two"` is pushed at the second dot, and `"three"` is pushed after the loop. `"four.five"` adds `"four"` and `"five"`, and `"six"` has no dot, so it is pushed whole at the end. `result` is `["one","two","three","four","five","six"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L), where L is the total number of characters, since each character is looked at once.
- Space: O(L) for the pieces in the answer.

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the final push after the inner loop loses the last piece of every word.
- Pushing without the length check adds empty strings for `"$easy$"` or `"x$$y"`.
- Only `separator` splits; the other symbols such as `,` or `|` are ordinary characters when they are not the separator.
- In some languages a split function treats its argument as a regular expression, where `.`, `|` and `$` are special.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | the non-empty pieces found so far, in order |
| `word` | the string currently being cut |
| `piece` | characters collected since the last separator |
| `ch` | the current character of `word` |
